//: The sources this plugin ships with, so nobody has to configure one to get started.
//maintainer: This file is the whole list. Edit it, run the tests, ship a release - that is the entire
process for adding a site, retiring one that died, or moving one that changed address. A
short copy is compiled in and used only when this file is missing or unreadable, so a
plugin folder that lost it still works and a typo in an edit does not leave an owner with
no sources at all.
A user never has to touch it. Their own sources live in their settings and are added on
top; a source of theirs with the same name replaces one of these outright, and a name in
disabledDefaultSources drops one. Their settings are never overwritten by an update and
this list is never copied into them - that is what lets one release fix a dead site for
everybody at once.
THE RULE FOR ADDING ONE: a source goes in enabled only when it has been seen to produce
rows this plugin can use - a name plus a magnet, an info hash, or a page that has one. A
site that answers 200 with a listing nobody can read is worse than no site at all: it
fills the sources page with a healthy-looking row that never yields a download, which is
exactly how one of these went unnoticed for weeks.
kind decides how the answer is read:
rss       - RSS or Atom. Ignores the query and hands over what it posted lately. A scene
feed carries release names and no torrents; that is the point. The names go
to the indexers, which is where the torrents are.
site      - an HTML search page, read by the reader named below.
apibay    - The Pirate Bay's JSON. name + info_hash + seeders, no markup, no challenge.
eztv-api  - EZTV's JSON. Accepts a search parameter and ignores it, so it is read whole
on the feed pass rather than asked about an episode.
yts       - YTS's JSON. Films only.
torznab   - Jackett or Prowlarr. Never a default: it needs the user's host and API key.
reader names the per-site reader; empty is the generic one, which suits any site that
keeps a magnet or a hashed .torrent link on its listing - and no large site does.
query decides how the terms are written into {query}:
words     - punctuation collapsed to single spaces, joined with +. The default, and what
nearly every search box tokenises best. A scene name sent with its dots
intact gets 1337x's error page rather than its results.
verbatim  - exactly as asked, punctuation and all.
slug      - lowercase, runs of anything else collapsed to a dash, for a site whose search
lives in the path. TorrentFunk answers a query with spaces with a redirect to
nothing, which reads exactly like a site with no results.
priority is a preference and a higher number is better: the scorer adds priority * 50 to a
release's score, the aggregator keeps the higher number when two sources offer one slot,
and the resolver takes the higher number when several sites hold one torrent.
gated says this source challenges every request, so a plain one is not worth making and
it goes straight to the browser. Leave it out unless the site really does: driving a
browser costs seconds, hundreds of megabytes, and on a server somebody is sitting in
front of it costs a window on their desktop. Eight of the addresses here answer plain
HTTP perfectly well. Gating is also a property of an address rather than of a site -
PreDB serves its feed openly and puts its search behind a challenge - so a source that
is not marked still reaches the browser the moment one of its addresses is challenged.
checked is when somebody last saw this source answer. No code reads it; it is here so the
next person knows how stale the list might be.

sources.name: PreDB
sources.note: Scene names in plain XML, no challenge. Names only - the torrents come from the indexers.

sources.name: srrDB
sources.note: Also names only. Served as text/html and is XML regardless.

sources.name: srrDB search
sources.note: Names, not torrents, and that is the point: it says what an episode from three weeks ago is actually called, and only a name like that is fit to put to an indexer. This is how a library that fell behind catches up - its gaps rolled out of every feed long ago.

sources.name: SceneSource
sources.note: Behind a Cloudflare challenge, which the plugin's own browser clears.

sources.name: EZTV latest
sources.note: Browse only. It takes a search parameter and ignores it, so it is read whole on the feed pass: everything on it is minutes old and arrives with a full magnet and seven trackers.

sources.name: The Pirate Bay
sources.note: Twelve rows for a real release name, each with an info hash and honest seeder counts. The website itself is a JavaScript shell with no results in it; this is what it calls.

sources.name: 1337x
sources.note: Proven end to end: scene name in, magnet out. The category-scoped address is the one that answers - a plain search with dots in the path returns their error page. No magnet on the listing, so the row is followed to its own page.

sources.name: LimeTorrents
sources.note: Publishes no magnet: every row links to a .torrent whose filename is the info hash, which is enough to build one. The generic reader handles it.

sources.name: TorrentBay
sources.note: Fifty rows and no magnet anywhere - not on the listing and not on the release page either. It answers a signed POST to its own ajax endpoint, made from inside the browser session that read the search page. Sorted by seeders so the best are on page one.

sources.name: EZTV
sources.note: Television only, which suits this plugin. Download links are hidden behind a button, so the row is followed to its own page.

sources.name: KickassTorrents
sources.note: Four anchors per row and three of them empty; the name is in cellMainLink, cut into highlighted fragments. Answered nothing for a scene name with dots in it, which is why the query style matters.

sources.name: TorrentGalaxy
sources.note: Sixteen rows for a real release name, no challenge in front of it. Its search lives in the path, where a plus is a plus - sent that way it read as one long word and the site looked like it had never heard of the episode. No magnet and no hash on the listing: the dozen forty-character hex strings on the page are element ids, and reading them as info hashes would grab twelve torrents that do not exist, so each row is followed to its own page.

sources.name: Torrentz2
sources.note: A meta search over other people's listings, twice written off here for having no magnet and no hash on the page. Both true, and beside the point: twenty results, each naming a release and its own page. Its titles carry the prefix of whichever site it copied, which the reader cuts.

sources.name: TorrentDownloads
sources.note: No hash on the listing, which is true of every large site here and means the magnet is one page further on. The first link is an advert for another site carrying the same terms, so rows are matched on the id every real release has.

sources.name: TorrentFunk
sources.note: Search lives in the path: a query with spaces gets a 301 to nothing, which reads exactly like a site with no results.

sources.name: Nyaa
sources.note: Anime, and an indexer written in XML: the query does reach its RSS and every item links a real torrent. On, because for anime it is the source that matters and the scene sites are not. It costs a request per episode on a library with no anime, which is a cheap thing to spend against an RSS - a missing anime source is not.

sources.name: YTS
sources.note: Films only, so off by default on a television library. yts.mx no longer resolves; .lt and .am both redirect to yts.gg, and their own answer says the base is moving again - which is why the address lives here and not in the code.
